generatedProse.concept-context: Across the School of Sport, the material a strategy has to cover is wide: physiology and biomechanics, research methods and statistics, coaching theory, policy and clinical practice. The two elements still drive the plan. Your use of time decides whether the topics you find hardest, perhaps the statistics behind a lab study or the mechanics of a movement, get more of it than the ones you already know. Identifying gaps means testing yourself on each topic, so a vague sense that biomechanics is weak becomes a clear target for your revision.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport and exercise science students have a month before the same exam, and the same notes.

Tom writes a timetable that gives every topic an equal block of time, from muscle physiology to the statistics of a lab report, and plans to re-read the notes for each. It looks organised. But Tom has not asked where his knowledge is weak, so the physiology he enjoys gets as much time as the statistics he dreads, and nothing tests whether the re-reading is working. This is a timetable, not a strategy.

Amara starts differently. She lists every topic the exam could cover, then does a quick test on each. The test shows that research methods and statistics are shaky while the core physiology is secure. She gives methods and statistics the most time, gives the secure physiology a short check, and fills each slot with an active technique. A week in, she re-tests and shifts the plan to where the gaps remain. This is a strategy.

Both students planned their month. Only Amara built the plan around time and gaps, which is what makes it a revision strategy.
generatedProse.summary: A revision strategy in the School of Sport is built on your use of time and your ability to identify gaps, whether the material is physiology, biomechanics, coaching theory or statistics. Its stages map the topics, test for gaps, budget time towards the weak areas, revise actively, then review and adjust. Holding to that under pressure is cognitive resilience. You can now recognise a real strategy and plan one for a sport module. The next lesson is about revising actively rather than passively.

check.body: In the worked example, what turned Amara's plan into a real revision strategy?

items.text: She tested herself, found that research methods and statistics were weak, and gave those topics the most time.
She planned to re-read every sport science topic for an equal block of time.
She started revising earlier than Tom did.
She made a neater, more colourful timetable than Tom.

feedback.correct: That's right. Amara built the plan around her gaps and spent time where it was needed, which is a strategy.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara built the plan around, rather than how it looked or when it started.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara's plan became a strategy because it was built around where her knowledge was weak and where time should go. A neat, equal, early timetable is not.
